## "It worked" is a measurement, not an observation

Ask an agent the same question five times and you can get five different answers. So the sentence
"it works" stops being something you notice and becomes something you measure. Ours ended up
enforcing four rules.

**One passing run proves nothing.** Every case runs several times and has to pass a majority. A
single green run tells you the failure rate is below 100%, which you already knew.

**One good day isn't a fix.** Two of our cases passed 3 out of 3 one week and 1 out of 3 the
next. Nothing had changed. We left them flagged as unreliable rather than declaring victory,
which is less satisfying and considerably more honest.

**Split the suite in two.** A lot of what you want to check needs no AI at all: does the
checklist advance, does the journey finish when the last item is ticked. Those tests are fast and
never flaky. Only the rest have to run the real agent, at real cost, at real speed.

**Keep the failures visible.** A known failure with a recorded pass rate is information. A
deleted test is a blind spot that looks identical to green.

And one more, which turned out to matter more than it sounds: **write down why a case passes.**
We had a rule whose position in the instructions — not its wording — was doing the work. The note

anyone remembered the detail.

## Put the guarantee in the code, not in the prompt

Our agent was misbehaving. There were two obvious ways to respond: write a better instruction, or
write the rule into the software so the mistake becomes impossible.

We did the first one. Repeatedly. The instruction grew, clause by clause, each clause added
because of a specific thing that had gone wrong. And the agent kept misbehaving.

That is worth sitting with, because the failure isn't obvious while it's happening. Every
individual edit to the instruction looks reasonable. Each one even helps a bit — the behaviour
gets rarer. Rarer is the trap. A rule that holds most of the time isn't a rule, it's a bug with a
low reproduction rate, and a low reproduction rate is worse than a high one, because it survives
your testing and finds your users instead.

What actually worked was moving the rule out of the prose and into deterministic code. Not a
firmer instruction — a function that cannot do the wrong thing.

The dividing line we ended up with: **the agent's job is what only a model can do.** Read the
question, work out what's being asked, summarise the material, choose the words. Everything
around that is bookkeeping — what's been done, what comes next, which record gets written — and
bookkeeping is what ordinary software has been reliable at for decades. Every time we handed
bookkeeping to the model because a sentence was faster to write than a function, we paid for it
later.

One limit caps how far this goes, and it's easy to miss. You can stop the agent from *doing* the
wrong thing. You cannot stop it from *saying* the wrong thing. Code protects what the system
records and what it displays; by the time a bad sentence exists, the user has already read it.
The wording still has to come out right the first time.

## Testing an agent needs statistics, not a look

For a while our loop was: agent misbehaves, change the code, try it by hand, looks fine, move on.

Two properties of agents break that loop, and they compound.

**Behaviour isn't proportional to the size of the edit.** In ordinary software, a small change
tends to have a small blast radius, and you can reason about where to look. Here a minor change
to an instruction or a tool can move behaviour somewhere you weren't watching, in a part of the
product you weren't touching.

**Behaviour isn't deterministic.** So checking it once tells you almost nothing. A single pass is
consistent with a case that passes nine times in ten and with a case that passes six times in
ten, and those are very different products.

Put together, manual testing after each change doesn't just miss things — it misses them
*silently*, and the miss then rides along under several more commits before anyone notices. Ours
ended in reverts, which is the expensive kind of debugging: you're no longer asking what's broken,

## Put the guarantee in the code, not in the prompt

Our agent was misbehaving. There were two obvious ways to respond: write a better instruction, or
write the rule into the software so the mistake becomes impossible.

We did the first one. Repeatedly. The instruction grew, clause by clause, each clause added
because of a specific thing that had gone wrong. And the agent kept misbehaving.

That's worth sitting with, because the failure isn't obvious while it's happening. Every
individual edit to the instruction looks reasonable. Each one even helps a little — the behaviour
gets rarer. Rarer is the trap. A rule that holds most of the time isn't a rule, it's a bug with a
low reproduction rate, and a low reproduction rate is worse than a high one, because it survives
your testing and finds your users instead.

What worked was moving the rule out of the prose and into deterministic code. Not a firmer
instruction — a function that cannot do the wrong thing.

The dividing line we ended up with: **the agent's job is what only a model can do.** Read the
question, work out what's being asked, summarise the material, choose the words. Everything
around that is bookkeeping — what's been done, what comes next, which record gets written — and
bookkeeping is what ordinary software has been reliable at for decades. Every time we handed
bookkeeping to the model because a sentence was faster to write than a function, we paid for it
later.

One limit caps how far this goes, and it's easy to miss. You can stop the agent from *doing* the
wrong thing. You cannot stop it from *saying* the wrong thing. Code protects what the system
records and what it displays; by the time a bad sentence exists, the user has already read it.
The wording still has to come out right the first time.

## When the user and the agent write to the same thing

Concept Buddy keeps one record of the onboarding journey: what's done, what's covered, where the
user is. The agent writes to it. So does the interface — a user can tick a checkbox without
saying anything to the agent at all. And the browser kept its own copy.

Both sides could write, so we merged them. That sentence is where it went wrong.

The bugs it produced were the kind that make users distrust the product:

- **Un-tick a box, and it ticks itself straight back on.** An older copy arrives, wins the merge,
  and undoes what the user just did in front of them.
- **Ticks made after the last message vanish on reload.** They existed only in the copy that
  wasn't authoritative.
- **The journey can't finish.** The completion check keeps looking at a record that keeps
  disagreeing with itself.

None of these is a model problem. The agent behaved impeccably throughout, on top of a record
that couldn't decide what was true.

The fix wasn't a smarter merge. Merging was the mistake — a merge is what you do when you've
declined to say who owns the data, and every merge rule we wrote was really a guess about which
writer had been more recently right.

So we picked an owner. **The journey lives in the browser.** The agent gets a copy at the start of
each turn and never keeps one between turns; it reads a snapshot, does its work, and hands
changes back. There's no second long-lived copy to drift.

And because a copy can still arrive late — a turn that started before the user's last click —
**the journey carries a version number that goes up on every user change.** Any copy that comes
back carrying an older version is ignored rather than merged. Late data is not new data.

That's the whole rule, and it's smaller than the merge logic it replaced: one owner, one copy per
turn, and a version that lets you throw away anything stale without having to work out what it
means.

## What Concept Buddy is

Starting somewhere new is mostly a queue of small questions. Where do I book time off, who
approves it, what's the name of that tool everyone keeps mentioning. None of them is hard. All of
them cost someone else's afternoon, and most new joiners sit on half of them rather than ask.

Concept Buddy is an onboarding assistant built for exactly that queue. It does two things at
once. It **walks a new colleague through five guided steps**, so onboarding has a shape rather
than being a folder of links. And it **answers everyday questions** about the company, its tools
and its policies, at whatever hour they come up.

Three properties make it more than a chat window over a search box.

**It's grounded in our own content.** Answers come out of the Welcome Book and Confluence, not
from a model's general impression of how companies work.

**Progress sticks.** It remembers where someone is in their onboarding, so the journey survives
closing the tab, and "what's left?" is a question it can actually answer.

**It runs in two places at once.** There's the conversation, and there's a dashboard showing the
journey — steps done, steps remaining — that updates as the conversation moves. The interface
adapts to where you are rather than sitting still beside the chat.

Why build it as an agent at all: it's available at all times, it lowers the barrier to asking a
question nobody wants to look silly asking, and it gives one consistent answer instead of five
half-remembered ones. It also saves the company real hours. And it was our first step toward
something larger — an internal agent for Concept, and the habit of building this way.

## How it's built

Worth two minutes, because a later section is about a bug you can't follow without this picture.

The frontend is **Next.js**. The backend is **FastAPI**, and the agent itself is built on
**Google ADK**, running on **Gemini**. Between them sits an interface layer — **CopilotKit** and
**AG-UI** — and that layer is the part worth paying attention to.

The agent is a single agent, not a team. It loads **agent skills**: separate procedures for
onboarding and for question-answering, pulled in when they're relevant rather than carried
permanently. Its knowledge comes from the Welcome Book and, over **MCP**, from Confluence. Its
memory of a conversation lives in the ADK session store.

The piece that matters later is the **journey state**: the record of which onboarding steps are
done. It is not private to the agent. The dashboard reads it, and a user can tick a step off
themselves without saying a word to the agent. **AG-UI** is what keeps user, application and agent
looking at the same journey across the stack.

So there are two parties who can change the same record — the person clicking, and the agent
acting — and a network between them. Hold on to that. Part 3 is largely the story of what that
costs and what we did about it.

## Connect the documentation before you write anything

We let the assistant build against a framework whose documentation wasn't connected to it. It
worked from what it already knew.

Nothing looked wrong. The code ran. The tests passed. That's the part worth dwelling on — there
was no failure to notice, no error to chase, nothing that would have made anyone stop and check.

What we'd actually got was code that wasn't aligned with the framework. It solved the problem in a
shape the framework didn't expect, and every addition after it had to fight that shape. The cost
arrived months later, as a large rewrite that never needed to happen.

An assistant works from its own trained knowledge unless you give it something better. It doesn't
announce when it's doing that. With a mature, widely-documented framework you'll often get away
with it. With anything new — and agent frameworks are all new — trained knowledge turns into
interpretation, and interpretation turns into confident misjudgement.

Three rules came out of it. **Connect the documentation first**, before any structural work.
**Read enough of it yourself** to recognise a wrong direction — you don't have to write the code,
you have to be able to say "that isn't how this framework does it." And **read the outputs**, not
just the summary of them, because risky edits are visible there and invisible in the summary.

Two prompts that do this work:

> "Please check the documentation and look for antipatterns."

> "How can we perform [X] according to the documentation?"

## Say where to stop

We asked for test cases. We didn't say what to test, why, or how much.

We got a testing setup wildly out of proportion to the project — and then had to go through it by
hand, cutting it back to the tests that covered the functionality we actually cared about.
Reducing it took real time, and none of that time bought anything.

The mechanism is simple once you've seen it. Without a stated purpose, the assistant has no way of
knowing where to stop, so it optimises for the only thing left: completeness. It isn't
over-engineering out of enthusiasm. It's answering the question you asked, which was unbounded.

The fix is to brief it the way you'd brief a junior developer joining the team. **Scope** — what
needs to be done. **Purpose** — why this is needed. **Limit** — where the boundary is. You'd never
say "write some tests" to a new colleague and walk away, and the negative half of a brief is
always the cheap half to give and the expensive half to undo.

In practice that's often two messages rather than one:

> **You:** "I want to check correct state sharing between the UI and the agent. Explore which test
> cases are relevant."
>
> **Assistant:** *[proposes cases]*
>
> **You:** "Write evals for these cases."

The same failure has a bigger sibling. We once built the entire agent in one go — onboarding,
dashboard, card rendering, the lot — as a single task spanning many files. What came out was one
enormous agent instruction with error sources scattered through it, and it had to be taken apart
in a dedicated rewrite.

A large request spreads the model's attention across many domains at once. A narrow one lets it
spend its full reasoning on every line it writes. Small, single-purpose tasks buy you more
attention per task and more control over the result.

## The four steps we ended up following every time

Both lessons above are really the same one arriving from different directions: the assistant does
best when it has been given something to work from and somewhere to stop. What that settled into
was a procedure — four steps, in order, on anything that wasn't trivial.

**Explore.** Let it read the code before it proposes anything.

> "I want to [X]. Explore which tool is currently responsible for fetching the MCP page."

**Plan.** Ask for the plan before the code.

> "Propose a plan for [X]."

**Question.** Ask why the alternatives were rejected. This is the step that gets skipped, and it's
the cheapest one — you're changing your mind before any code exists. It also doubles as a
detector: if the answer to "why not the other way?" is vague, the plan is vague.

> "Check if this aligns with [doc reference]. Why don't we do [X] instead?"

**Verify.** Check the result yourself. "The assistant says it works" is not a result.

> "Run [the eval / the browser] and show me it works."
>
> "[X] seems off — did we break something?"

Nothing here is exotic, and that's rather the point. Explore, plan, question, verify is how you'd
work with a capable colleague who is fast, literal, and entirely willing to build the wrong thing
extremely well.

## Seven agents, then one

Our first architecture was a team. Seven agents: one for each of the five onboarding steps, one
handling user questions, and an orchestrator on top deciding who should answer.

This is the design everyone reaches for, and it's easy to see why. It mirrors how you'd split the
work between people. Each agent gets a small, clear job. It looks like separation of concerns.

It was overkill, and it was messy. The orchestrator became the problem: it confused the order of
the onboarding steps, and it couldn't reliably tell when a message was a question for the Q&A
agent rather than a step to continue. So the failures landed in the least debuggable place
possible — not inside any agent, but in the routing between them, where there's no single
conversation to read back and work out what went wrong.

What replaced it was **one agent, plus agent skills, plus state**.

The state carries onboarding progress, so the agent always knows where the user is without anyone
having to tell it. The skills carry the procedures — one for onboarding, one for Q&A — loaded when
they're relevant rather than crammed into a single permanent instruction. Same separation of
concerns. No routing layer to get it wrong, and one conversation to read when something does.

The rule we'd give now: if you have **multiple processes inside one instruction**, that's what
agent skills are for. Separate the procedures, keep the agent.

Reach for a second agent when you need something a skill genuinely can't give you: a **separate
context window**, **true concurrency**, a **different trust or tool boundary**, or a **different
outcome** from the first agent's. Those are real reasons. "These are conceptually different jobs"
is not one — that's a skill.

Mark up `concept-buddy.md` directly — the file you're reading. Drop a marker anywhere, inline at
the end of a line or on its own:

| marker | means |

| `@more` | thin, needs expanding |
| `@why` | unclear, or justify this claim |
| `@note` | anything else |
